name: Yusuf Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI companies, employers, unions, parties and government, and this conversation is confidential. What sort of day did you have at work yesterday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The printer jammed as I was checking a grocer's year-end accounts, so I spent the first hour comparing the stock sheet on screen with a paper tally. I'm 43 and an experienced accountant at Mill Street Accounts, about average at the work; I have a bachelor's degree and a professional accountancy qualification. I enjoy finding why a shop's margin changed, but explaining the same missing invoice three times can wear me down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who depends on your pay, and how do new tools fit into that day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Leena works as a pharmacy assistant, and our children are nine and twelve; the mortgage comes out just after the school lunch payments. My pay is low for this job, we have less than one month of expenses saved, and there are few accounting jobs nearby. I use AI now and then to draft a client question after someone else has tried it, then check the stock figures myself. I believe workers need a say before employers change their jobs, and public support has a place when wages disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the shop owners a quicker invoice sort is welcome if we can still show them the source. I'd also say the firm should share any saved time with the people who do the checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The job probably stays, but our mortgage is already tight on my low wage and Leena's pharmacy hours. Less than a month saved means a late pay cheque would still send us to family for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reconciling grocer stock and tax figures using the current checks, and continue the occasional AI draft without client numbers. Starting this payday, we'd put thirty a week into a separate mortgage buffer by making soup at home instead of buying lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious even in the mild picture. The bank does not wait for a technology story to become interesting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who could help if a cheque were late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leena's sister could lend us one mortgage payment, but I would hate asking. I'd rather build the buffer a little each week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the staff about the sorter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the elected staff representative to get the error count before any target changes. I won't claim a saved hour until someone has checked the bad invoices.

I would promise clients a **source trail** behind sorted invoices.

do: Keep reconciling **grocer stock** and tax figures with the firm’s current human checks.

Ask the **staff representative** for error counts before targets change.
feel: He feels **anxious** about mortgage payments despite a stable job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the staff representative to ask for paid training and a written plan for the accounts team. Software that writes and checks returns changes what we're paid to do, even if nobody is dismissed on day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the partners to cut at least one of my paid days when software handles stock checks and tax letters. I am experienced but ordinary, not the one they would keep at any price, and our savings would not cover a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a paid test of the firm's tool on twelve closed shop accounts, with a senior reviewing errors, and put the request through the staff representative. In the first year of steady change, if my paid week drops below four days, I'd apply for posted accounts roles at the one other firm on the bus route while keeping paid hours at Mill Street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because a lost day would put the mortgage at risk. A training day is useful only if it is paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm refuses the paid test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the current accounts work and ask the representative to record that refusal. I could read the instructions at home, but I would not upload shop records into a tool nobody has approved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a new job have to pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need a written wage and start date that cover the mortgage and Leena's reduced pharmacy shifts if she collects the children. A posted vacancy is not the same as a confirmed offer.

fieldNote: His training request is **paid and supervised**; refusal means keeping current work, not unpaid client testing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team that full AGI in 2028 can do the thinking parts of our tax desk, and we need notice before hours are cut. I'd ask who signs a return when a client disputes the machine's number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The 2028 date reaches my desk, not the robot date around 2031. I expect Mill Street to cut at least one accountant and could be the one, while Leena's pharmacy counter work might face robots later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop the children's paid music lessons for a term and add the sixty monthly fee to our mortgage buffer now. In the first year after 2028, if my post ends, I'd apply for advertised salaried stock-control work at the local wholesalers and request income support if eligible; I would keep the buffer for the loan while looking for a written wage offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. A month of savings cannot carry a mortgage through a long job search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about music?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the lessons pause while we protect the house, and that we'd restore them when the buffer covers a full mortgage payment. I would still practise with them at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to another town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a written salary offer with a start date and enough pay after travel to cover the mortgage. I would not take the children from school because a wholesaler says it may advertise.

say: I would ask for **advance notice** before AGI cuts hours.
I would demand a **named signer** for disputed returns.
think: My **desk job** could be cut when AGI arrives in 2028.
Leena’s **counter hours** may face robots around 2031.
do: Pause **sixty-monthly music** until one mortgage payment is saved.
Add **sixty monthly** to the mortgage buffer now.
Seek **posted salaried stock-control** after job loss; move only with written start and mortgage-covering pay after travel.
feel: He feels **alarmed** because one month saved cannot carry the mortgage.
S2.quote: A month of savings cannot carry a mortgage through a long job search.
fieldNote: He makes a **specific family cut**, but promises home practice and a clear condition for resuming lessons.
He separates **2028 desk loss** from later counter robots and would request income help only if eligible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives the staff and partners time to agree on paid training for work that still brings fees. A last-minute course list would not keep anyone in a home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 in 2031, I'd still be paying the mortgage, and AGI could do the accounts checks I know well. Leena's hands-on pharmacy work may face robots around 2034, so we need a plan for both wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the staff representative for a funded placement in inventory control at a wholesaler next year, only if a firm offers paid hours and Mill Street keeps my wage during the trial. In the first year after 2031, if my accounts hours are cut, I'd apply for posted salaried inventory jobs and keep any paid Mill Street hours until a written start date and wage are confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but five years lets us test a paid route before losing wages. I won't ask Leena to carry an unpaid experiment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn on that placement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd follow warehouse stock counts, trace spoiled goods and see which entries reach the monthly accounts. I'd need someone at the warehouse to supervise the first count because paper records and shelves do not always agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no paid placement is offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing shop accounts and ask the representative to put the refusal in the meeting notes. We would still save thirty weekly; I would not pay for a private course without an advertised salaried job.

I would ask the staff representative to **record refusals**.

Leena’s **pharmacy work** may face robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the firm ten years is time to build a paid service for shop owners who want a person to explain stock losses. The workers should see the price and the hours before anyone promises jobs from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036, the children may have left school, but we could still owe on the mortgage. A decade of earnings may let us pay down debt; AGI reaches my thinking work in 2036, while robots around 2039 may also affect Leena's pharmacy shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add one hundred a month to mortgage principal only while both wages hold, and ask Mill Street for a paid trial of quarterly stock-loss meetings with three grocers, with fees going to the firm. In the first year after 2036, if two grocers renew at fees covering my paid hours, I'd stay; if not, I'd apply for posted salaried wholesaler roles and keep any funded firm work until a written offer starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious rather than calm. Ten years helps. A mortgage at 53 still needs wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show a grocer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare spoiled stock with purchase orders, then ask the owner which loss is normal and which can be stopped. If nobody pays for the second meeting, the service is a cost, not a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take early retirement if the loan shrinks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we cannot retire on less than a month's savings today. I'd rather pay down the debt and work while there is a paid role.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a tax desk cut could reach our mortgage before we have one month saved. Advance notice, paid training and an actual salaried opening would help. I can live with a new tool; I cannot pay the lender with an unfunded promise.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays for a worker to learn inventory while the old job is still paying the mortgage. A course offered after the wage ends is a door with no floor behind it.

headlineQuote: A course offered after the wage ends is a door with no floor behind it.
portrait: Yusuf, **43**, is an experienced, average-skilled accountant at Mill Street with a bachelor’s degree and professional qualification.
His **low pay**, under-one-month cushion and few nearby firms strain a mortgage shared with Leena and two school-age children.
He uses AI **occasionally after colleagues** and asks the staff representative for paid training and clear decisions.
He fears **2028 desk cuts** most, then tests funded inventory work and a firm-owned grocer service on longer timelines.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut his tax wage before the household saves one mortgage payment.
whatWouldHelp: **Advance notice**, paid training and an actual salaried opening would give him a usable path.
